sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. [c. 2020-2022]. Porapora River. NewGuineaWorld (Santa Fe Institute), Families > Keram and Ramu Rivers > Ramu River > Porapora River (with empty subpages Abu, Gorovu). Web publication; the Internet Archive snapshot of 2022-10-06 (live site now requires Google sign-in).
sources.note: Reconstructs proto-Porapora River with 14-15 consonants and 4 vowels (*i *ʉ *u *a) and gives complete initial/medial/final correspondence tables with Gorovu reflexes (e.g. *mb > Gorovu w, *ŋg > g, *p > [p ɸ f], final *r + echo vowel). The only prosodic remark is diachronic: sub-initial consonants 'have become initial in all three languages due to the mutual loss of destressed initial high central vowel /*ʉ/' (i.e. initial *ʉ was unstressed). No synchronic statement of where Gorovu stress falls, and 'No information about Porapora River verbal morphology is currently available'. WORDLIST-ONLY S…

sources.citation: Brooks, Joseph D. 2018. Realis and irrealis: Chini verb morphology, clause chaining, and discourse. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara (ch. 2.5 'Chini and the Ramu family', pp. 69-87, surveys all Ramu languages and their documentation).

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 2007. Australasia and the Pacific. In Christopher Moseley (ed.), Encyclopedia of the world's endangered languages, 425-577. London: Routledge. Entry 'Gorovu (or Yerani) [32]', p. 492.
sources.note: No phonology content. Gives only family-level Ramu morphological typology (simpler morphology than Sepik languages, little or no person marking on verbs, frequent regular noun plurals, noun classes/gender rare, no sentence-medial verb forms), no literacy, 50 speakers in 1981 now twenty or less, shift to Banaro.
sources.venue: Encyclopedia of the world's endangered languages

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 2001. Language endangerment in the insular Greater Pacific area, and the New Guinea area in particular. In Andrew Pawley, Malcolm Ross & Darrell Tryon (eds), The boy from Bundaberg: studies in Melanesian linguistics in honour of Tom Dutton (Pacific Linguistics 514), 383-398. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. DOI 10.15144/PL-514.383
sources.note: Nothing. Gorovu occurs once in the chapter, as a bare entry in the endangerment listing (Papuan, 20 speakers, East Sepik Province, class 'moribund'); the chapter is an endangerment survey with no linguistic data for any language. a full-text search for stress/accent over the whole text: 'stress', 'tone', 'tonal', 'accent', 'pitch', 'prosod' all 0 hits; even 'Ramu' does not occur. Reopening it settles round 1's open pointer: silent, as round 1 predicted.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, John A. 1975. The languages of the Madang District, Papua New Guinea (Pacific Linguistics B-41). Canberra: Australian National University. vi+154 pp.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content: a checklist/gazetteer with classification, village lists, populations, maps and an index. Gorovu appears in the introduction ('spoken.. only in part of the village, as in the case of 01 Gorovu'), the Porapora Family listing (01 Gorovu 50, Bangapela) and the indexes. The introduction refers readers to Z'graggen 1971 and forthcoming comparative wordlist volumes for linguistic material.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1973. Sepik languages: checklist and preliminary classification (Pacific Linguistics B-25). Canberra: ANU.http://hdl.handle.net/1885/146478
sources.note: Entry 133 Gorovu (Yerani), printed p.38: village Bangapella, 'Test DCL71 (Parana/Bangapella)', merger with Banaro-speaking Bangapella; under 135 Aion renames Agoan as 'Grass Family'. Only a generic 'Sepik-type phonology' remark for the phylum; nothing on Gorovu stress.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J. A. 1971. Classificatory and typological studies in languages of the Madang District (Pacific Linguistics C-19). Canberra: ANU.http://hdl.handle.net/1885/146580
sources.note: Published version of the thesis. Gorovu sec. 2.23.41.2, printed p.87 (village, 50 speakers, closer to Adjora than Banaro); Agoan typological features p.87-88 are morphological only. Printed p.6: same sentence that stress marking is omitted because stress patterning is not established. Silent on Gorovu stress.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, John A. 1970. Languages of the Western Madang District. In S. A. Wurm & D. C. Laycock (eds), Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell (Pacific Linguistics C-13), 1271-1292. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing for Gorovu or for the Ramu Phylum: the article is a summary of the 1969 thesis giving research history, the list/classification of languages (Gorovu = 69 Gv, Agoan Family, speaker figure in the chart), a map, and phylum-level typological notes. The Ramu Phylum notes (p.1280) are purely morphological (quoted); the only prosodic remark in the paper, 'None of the languages appears to be tonal', belongs to list B (Adelbert Range Phylum), not to Ramu. No word 'stress'/'accent' anywhere in the text; no Gorovu forms.
sources.venue: Pacific linguistic studies in honour of Arthur Capell (Pacific Linguistics C-13)

sources.citation: Z'graggen, John A. 1969. Classificatory and typological studies in languages of the Madang District, New Guinea. PhD thesis, Australian National University. x+335 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/1885/130077
sources.note: Gorovu (lg 69 'Gv') appears only in sec. 2.23.41.2 (printed p.167: location, 45 speakers, expected to die out) and in Gv rows of pronoun/typological tables (pp.182-186, 319-320). Printed p.13 (p.22), for the whole survey: 'The marking of stress has been omitted, since the stress patterning has not been well established yet.' Nothing on Gorovu stress.
